newsitem.title: ITALY: Report of board shake-up adds to Olivetti crisis.
newsitem.headline: Report of board shake-up adds to Olivetti crisis.

text.p: Italy's Olivetti group on Wednesday said it could not answer key questions from market regulators about its troubled affairs and a newspaper report said the company could be heading for another board shake-up.

The loss-making information technology and telecoms group, whose shares have slumped to a record low, came up with answers on Wednesday to most of 16 detailed questions put to it by bourse watchdog Consob about the state of its finances.
But the company said in a statement that it could not divulge confidential information about negotiations underway on future divestments or strategic accords.

It also said it could not state its consolidated financial situation for the end of August 1996 until the first week of October. This was because of the need to gather "data coming from around 200 companies operating in the group."

Olivetti, one of Italy's entrepreneurial success stories of the 1980s, has been caught in a snowballing crisis involving doubts about the accuracy of its first-half accounts since the shock resignation of chairman Carlo De Benedetti on September 3.
He was forced off the board after 18 years as chairman in a dramatic showdown with chief executive Francesco Caio, who formerly served as his personal assistant.
Industrial sources said Olivetti was expected to hold a board meeting on Wednesday afternoon with an unspecified agenda.

Earlier the Paris-based International Herald Tribune reported the Olivetti board would meet to discuss a management shakeup which could result in the ousting of Caio. However an Olivetti spokeswoman said she was unable to comment.

Caio, 39, new chairman Antonio Tesone and De Benedetti himself are being investigated by magistrates in Olivetti's home town of Ivrea who suspect the company may have issued misleading statements about its affairs, judicial sources say.

The inquiry has contributed to a wave of panic selling of Olivetti shares which slumped 9.91 percent to close at 465.3 lire (30 cents) on Tuesday, a new record low, after being halted repeatedly as they tested a 10 percent limit on price movements.
Trading in the stock was due to start later than the rest of the Milan bourse on Wednesday, with the open set for 1010 GMT.
The stock market council said this would give the market time to digest the 16 answers furnished by Olivetti.

The biggest blow so far to the company's credibility came on September 4, the day after De Benedetti's dramatic exit, when Olivetti director general Renzo Francesconi resigned in a dispute with Caio over the first half results.

Stock market regulator Consob has questioned Caio and Francesconi over the results and on Monday night published a list of 16 questions about Olivetti's balance sheet and a demand for answers to be provided within 24 hours.
Olivetti's financial exposure has spiralled since the group completed a massive 2.26 trillion lire ($1.48 billion) rights issue at the end of last year.
The company said its net debt at the end of June totalled 1.26 trillion but analysts say that interest charges paid by the company suggest that it may really owe far more.
